title: The tight-query key-value mix on six server cores instead of eight
description: The same bursty key-value front end as w13 (lookups, puts with occasional 120 us flushes, replica syncs routed through the put path, 68 us queries due in 300 us, 120 us multigets, batch, scans and 2 us lease renewals), with the same hints, but the service now runs on 6 cores instead of 8, as when a cluster manager shrinks a service's allocation to free cores for batch work, and traffic is scaled down by the same factor so each core is exactly as busy as before. With fewer cores, a lookup more often finds every core busy with a long request and more requests queued on its own core, so the order in which waiting requests run matters more. A scheduler that ranks lookups behind puts, syncs or queries that turned urgent now costs them more waiting than on w13.
changed_from_previous: w13 on 6 server cores instead of 8 (guaranteed and spinning 6), with every load level multiplied by 6/8 so the load per core is unchanged; mix, work, hints, deadlines, bursts and 16 connections unchanged.
notes: Real shapes. The core change follows cluster managers that right-size a latency-critical service's CPU allocation to raise utilization (Google Autopilot, Rzadca et al., EuroSys 2020) or take its cores for batch work while load allows (Heracles, Lo et al., ISCA 2015; Caladan itself, Fried et al., OSDI 2020): the same service then serves the same load per core on fewer cores. The mix is w13's, unchanged: a key-value front end with lookups and batched multigets (memcache at Facebook, Nishtala et al., NSDI 2013), writes that occasionally wait for a log flush (LSM stores such as RocksDB, Cao et al., FAST 2020), replica syncs from peers (Raft-style log replication, as in etcd), and lease renewals (Chubby KeepAlives, Burrows, OSDI 2006). Its weights, work sizes and the 10x query-to-lookup ratio were invented in w2-w13, not taken from a trace; real long-tailed service is approximated by constant kinds plus the puts' bimodal flushes. Hints are w13's (what that server sets by routing syncs through the put handler and multigets through the lookup handler); no new relabelling. Capacity, at 99.6 iterations per us (calibration.json): fake work per request get 0.922 + put 1.934 + query 27.651 + sync 5.422 + multiget 5.422 + batch 6.145 + scan 6.145 + lease 0.171 = 53.81 us (5359.4 iterations); 6 / 53.81 us = 111.5k req/s (103.8k with the calibrated 4 us per request). Levels are sized from measured light-load medians (gen 10 lesson): 5359.4 / 83 iterations per us + 1 us = 65.57 us per request, 6 / 65.57 us = 91.5k req/s. The levels are w13's per-core levels times 6/8 (w13 equivalents 35k, 70k, 90k, 95k, 97.5k, 100k): 26.25k/52.5k/67.5k/71.25k/73.125k/75k are 28.7/57.4/73.8/77.9/79.9/82.0% of 91.5k, and 75k is w13's headline load per core (100k on 8 cores). The top is kept at w13's headline, not above, because the probe reads the two busiest levels and both must pass the headline rule: on w13 fifo's overall median was 116.5 us at 100k and 147.5 at 105k against a limit of 136.5 (1.5 x 91). A queueing simulation of this mix (central queue, 100 us time slice, bursts), matched to w13's fifo medians on 8 cores within 8 us, puts 6 cores at matched load per core 2-13 us higher (75k: about 120-130 us; 73.125k about 110-120), so 75k should be the headline, 73.125k the fallback. Bursts as in w13 (4000 us, duty 0.25, factor 2; busy-phase rate at 75k is 120k req/s). Deadlines as in w13: leases 100 us, queries 300 (4.4x), gets, puts and syncs 400, multigets 1200; all at least 3x the kind's work. The FIFO penalty is w13's: gets wait behind queries, syncs, flushes and multigets (w13 fifo get p99 657 vs 26.5 at light load). Why the champion has headroom: p13 sjf_upper's unit is read per core from HIGH deadlines, which do not depend on the core count, so it decides as on w13 (unit 4); there its get runqueue-wait p99 was 125.4 us at 100k against 84.5 on w12 with the same unit, the gap being queries that turn urgent and pass gets (about 24 us, gen 12 report) and the puts' and syncs' order. On 6 cores each ordering mistake costs more, because a core's queue is pooled with fewer neighbours: in the simulation, the unavoidable wait for a free core under an ideal lookups-first order rises from 35 to 41 us at p99 (+18%), and fifo's get wait p99 by 8%. Prediction at 75k (headline): fifo get p99 about 680-760 us (w13 657), fifo overall median about 120-130 us; sjf_upper get p99 about 225-260 us (w13 208.5), get runqueue-wait p99 about 140-175 us (w13 125.4), so a runqueue share of about 0.62-0.68 (w13 0.60); steals above w13's 25.9% of picks; put and sync p99 about 5-15% above w13. At 26.25k every policy's get p99 stays near 25 us. Server hint map unchanged from w13. No run.py changes are needed.
